t: K-Similar Strings — BFS on String States with Pruning
o: We need the minimum number of swaps of two positions in `s1` to turn it into its anagram `s2`. This is a shortest-path problem where each string is a node and an edge connects strings differing by one swap. **Example 1:** "ab" -> swap(0,1) -> "ba", so k = 1. **Example 2:** "abc" -> swap(0,1) -> "bac" -> swap(1,2) -> "bca", so k = 2. Constraints (length ≤ 20, alphabet of only 6 letters) mean many positions already match and duplicates are common; a naive BFS over all swaps would blow up, but pruning to *useful* swaps keeps the state space tiny.
k: Minimum number of swaps = shortest path in a graph whose nodes are strings and edges are single swaps, solvable with BFS.
Only swap s1[i] with a position j > i where s2[i] == s1[j] and s1[j] != s2[j]; swapping into an already-correct position never helps.
Memoizing visited states is essential because duplicate letters create many paths to the same intermediate string.

a.i: Treat every reachable string as a graph node; BFS guarantees the first time we reach s2 we used the minimum number of swaps. From each state try every pair (i, j). This works but explores many useless swaps (e.g., swapping two equal letters or breaking correct positions), making it slow for n = 20.
s: Start BFS from s1 with distance 0.
For each dequeued string, if it equals s2 return the current distance.
Try all pairs (i, j) with i < j; swap characters and enqueue unseen results.
Track visited strings in a set to avoid revisiting states.
a.t: Exponential in the worst case — each level can branch up to O(n^2) ways over potentially many distinct states.
a.sp: O(number of distinct states × n) for the visited set and queue.

a.i: A good swap must place some character into its correct target position. So at each state, find the first index i where cur[i] != s2[i]; it suffices to swap cur[i] with any later position j holding s2[i]. Swapping two already-matching positions or moving a wrong character elsewhere without fixing one is provably never beneficial for optimality. Combined with memoization this prunes the search dramatically and passes easily for n ≤ 20.
s: BFS from s1; when popping a state, skip all leading indices where cur matches s2.
Let i be the first mismatched index; for each j > i with cur[j] == s2[i], swap and enqueue if unvisited.
Return the BFS depth when a state equals s2.
Use a hash set of visited strings to deduplicate states caused by repeated letters.
a.t: Hard to bound tightly, but empirically near O(k · n · S) where S is the (small, pruned) number of reachable states; vastly faster than brute force since each expansion considers at most n candidate swaps instead of n².
a.sp: O(S · n) for the visited set and queue, where S is the number of distinct pruned states.

w: In an interview, present Approach 1 first to establish the shortest-path framing, then immediately propose the pruning insight: always fix the leftmost mismatched index using a swap that places the right character there. Choose Approach 2 as the final solution — it comfortably handles n = 20. Common pitfalls: forgetting the visited set (exponential blowup from duplicate letters), allowing swaps that break already-correct positions, and scanning for j starting at 0 instead of i+1 (harmless but wasteful). Edge cases: s1 == s2 returns 0; identical adjacent letters must not generate duplicate branches. Follow-ups: prove why fixing the first mismatch is safe (any optimal sequence can be reordered so its first swap fixes the earliest mismatched position), or solve with IDDFS/A* for memory-constrained variants.
